**Introduction **

Because of inheritance, a child class can automatically receive the attributes and methods of its parent class. This helps reduce code repetition and keeps programs organized. However, the inherited method is sometimes too general and does not fully match the child class's specific needs. For example,  an Animal class with a method **make\_sound()** that prints “Some sound.” A Dog class that inherits from Animal would want to change this method so it prints “Woof” instead, because that better represents a dog. Since child classes often represent more specialized versions of the parent, they may need to change or override how a method works. This is where method overriding becomes important.

Method overriding occurs when a child class provides its own version of a method already defined in the parent class. The method name stays the same, but the behavior is different. In Python, this is done by redefining the method in the child class using the same method name and parameters. When the method is called using an object of the child class, the child’s version runs instead of the parent’s version.

This study guide presents examples demonstrating how method overriding works in code. Through these examples, you will understand how overriding allows programmers to customize inherited behavior while still enjoying the advantages of inheritance.  
 

   
**Module Learning Objectives **

1. Explain method overriding in a child class

**Key Concepts and Learning Activities **

***1.1. Method Overriding***   

Method overriding in object-oriented programming is a mechanism that allows a child class to provide a specific implementation of a method already defined in the parent class.  

Let us use the Animal class from the previous module as the first example to demonstrate method overriding. Refer to the class diagram below for the illustration. 

The Animal class has the methods **eat()** and **sleep()**. Then it adds another method, **make\_sound()**, designed to produce a sound. Since Dog and Cat are child classes of Animal, they inherit the make\_sound() method. However, dogs and cats make different sounds. Hence, each child class must create its own version of **make\_sound()** to display the specific sound for that animal. 

 ![][image1]

***Example 1:***

Let's translate the class diagram into Python code:  

| Python:  \# Parent class class Animal:     def \_\_init\_\_(self, name):         self.name \= name     def eat(self):         print(self.name,"is eating.")     def sleep(self):         print(self.name, "is sleeping.")     def make\_sound(self):         print(self.name, "makes a sound") \# Child classes override the inherited method make\_sound() class Dog(Animal):     def make\_sound(self):       print(self.name, "says Woof\!") class Cat(Animal):     def make\_sound(self):       print(self.name, "says Meow\!") \# Create objects animal1 \= Animal("Generic Animal") dog1 \= Dog("Bruno") cat1 \= Cat("Kitty") \# Output the animal make\_sound animal1.make\_sound() dog1.make\_sound() cat1.make\_sound()  |
| :---- |

Dog and Cat each define their own version of the **make\_sound()** method. They introduce a different print statement within the method, without changing the method's name or parameters. 

From    **print(self.name, "makes a sound")**  to   
             **print(self.name, "says Woof\!")**   in Dog class and   
 **print(self.name, "says Meow\!")**  in Cat class.

When a Dog object is created, and the method is called, it uses the Dog class's implementation. The same happens with a Cat object, as shown in the output. 

| ![][image2] |
| :---- |

Notice how Dog and Cat use the same inherited method, **make\_sound()**, but each provides its own version of that method. This is method overriding. 

Now, take a look at how the method **make\_sound()** is called directly on each object using separate statements: 

| The code that executes the method make\_sound() animal1.make\_sound() dog1.make\_sound() cat1.make\_sound() |
| :---- |

This method can also be called inside a loop, as in your lesson in Grade 8\. 

| Using a loop to execute the method make\_sound() in each class \#Use for loop to execute the method make\_sound() of each object animals \= \[animal1, dog1, cat1\] for animal in animals:   animal.make\_sound()  |
| :---- |

All objects are placed in a list, and the method is executed in a for loop. Even though the loop variable is named animal, Python automatically determines which version of make\_sound() to run based on the actual type of each object.

***Example 2\.   Method Overriding in a Simple Library Management System***  
                    ***(using the super() built-in function)***

Let us implement method overriding in the Library Management System from the previous module by overriding the Publication parent class's **display\_info()** method.

![][image3]

The three versions of the method **display\_info()** are provided: 

|  Parent class:  Publication   def display\_info(self):         print("Title:", self.\_\_title)         print("Author:", self.\_\_author)  Child class:  Book  def display\_info(self):         super().display\_info()         print("Number of Pages:", self.\_\_number\_of\_pages)  Child class: Magazine     def display\_info(self):         super().display\_info()         print("Issue Number:", self.\_\_issue\_number)  |
| :---- |

The Publication parent class's **display\_info()** method displays the **title** and **author.**

The child classes override this method by adding their own specific attribute to the output:   
	**print("Number of Pages:", self.\_\_number\_of\_pages)    //**in the Book Class

	**print("Issue Number:", self.\_\_issue\_number)                //**in the Magazine Class   

while still including the title and author information from the parent class's **display\_info()** with the use of the super() built-in function.  
	  
**super().display\_info()**

**super()** in Python is a built-in function used in inheritance to call a method from a parent class inside a child class,  just like in **super().\_\_init\_\_(),** which calls the "parent's" version of the **\_\_init\_\_()**   method, which you have seen in the previous module. It allows the child class to reuse and extend the parent class's behavior without completely replacing it.

Without using method overriding, displaying the book details requires calling the inherited method **display\_info()** and then adding a line of code to print the number of pages of a book:

| ![][image4] |
| :---: |

Using method overriding makes the code cleaner and more straightforward. Instead of adding an extra line of code outside the method, the specific detail \- such as the number of pages \- is directly within the overridden **display\_info()** of the child class. 

| ![][image5] |
| :---: |

The child class provides a specific implementation of the method **display\_info()**, tailored to its requirements, without changing the inherited method's name and parameters. 

The details of each object can be printed using a for loop instead of calling the method on each object individually, as demonstrated in the following code.

### **Key takeaways** 

Method overriding is a feature of object-oriented programming in which a child class provides its own version of a method from its parent class. This lets different classes use the same method name but do different things, which helps keep programs flexible and organized.

Method overriding happens only when one class inherits from another. The child class's method must use the same name and parameters as the parent’s method. This way, the child class can properly override or extend the parent's method.

In Python, you can use the super() function to call a method from the parent class while working in the child class. This lets you reuse the parent's code and add new features to the child class, without having to rewrite the whole method.

Overall, method overriding lets you change inherited methods to suit your needs without changing the parent class. This makes your code easier to reuse, adapt, and maintain.
